Description of file system navigation
● The ls command is used to list the contents of a directory.
● By default, it shows the names of files and directories in the current working
directory.
● It can be modified with options (like -l, -a, etc.) to provide additional details about
the files, such as file permissions, sizes, and hidden files.
● The command l is not a standard command in Linux by itself. However, it may be
an alias for ls -l in many systems.
● If defined as an alias, it would typically list files in the long format, displaying
detailed information such as permissions, owner, group, size, and last modification
date.
● The ls -la command provides a detailed list of all files and directories, including
hidden files (those beginning with a dot .).
● It displays information in a long format, including file permissions, number of links,
owner, group, size, and timestamp of the last modification.
● In contrast, ls alone only shows the names of non-hidden files and directories in a
simple list format.
● The pwd command stands for "print working directory."
● It displays the full path of the current directory in which the user is located.
● It helps users understand their location within the file system hierarchy.
● The cd command stands for "change directory."
● It is used to navigate between directories in the file system.
● Users can specify the path to the target directory, allowing them to move up, down,
or to a different branch of the directory structure.
● Common usages include cd .. to move to the parent directory and cd ~ to return to
the home directory.
Description of basic commands for viewing current user information
● The id command shows user and group identity information for the current user or
a specified user.
● It displays the user ID (UID), the primary group ID (GID), and a list of supplementary
group memberships
● Useful for understanding permissions and access control in a Linux environment.
● The getent command retrieves entries from administrative databases, such as
users, groups, or hosts.
● It can access various database types configured in /etc/nsswitch.conf.
● Example: getent passwd displays user account information, similar to cat
/etc/passwd.

● The whoami command displays the username of the current user executing the
command.
● It tells you exactly who you are logged in as at that moment.
● In contrast, the who command shows a list of all users currently logged into the
system, along with their terminal, login time, and originating IP address or
hostname.
● The who command displays a list of users currently logged into the system.
● It provides details such as Username, Terminal name, Login time, and Source (IP
address or hostname) from where the user is connected
● Useful for monitoring active users and system usage.
● The w command displays information about currently logged-in users and their
activities.
● It provides Username, Terminal, Login time, Idle time, and the command currently
being executed by each user
● It offers a more detailed view compared to the who command, allowing
administrators to see what users are doing.
Description of processes management for Linux
● The ps command displays a snapshot of current processes running on the system.
● It provides information such as Process ID (PID), terminal associated with the
process, CPU and memory usage, state of the process, and the command that
started the process.
● Common options include ps aux for a detailed view of all processes or ps -ef for a
full-format listing.
● The top command provides a dynamic, real-time view of processes running on the
system, updating every few seconds.
● It displays CPU and memory usage, system load, running processes, and their
statuses.
● Unlike ps, which gives a static snapshot, top allows users to monitor system
performance and resource usage interactively.
● htop is an enhanced version of top, offering a more user-friendly interface with
color-coded output.
● It allows users to scroll through the process list, search for processes, and sort by
various columns interactively.
● Users can also send signals (like kill) to processes directly from the interface, making
it easier to manage processes.
● The pgrep command searches for processes based on name and other attributes
and returns their Process IDs (PIDs).

-- 59 of 132 --

51 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
● It is useful for finding PIDs without listing all processes manually, using patterns or
regular expressions.
● Common options include pgrep -u username to find processes owned by a specific
user.
● The kill command is used to send signals to processes, typically to terminate them.
● It requires a PID as an argument, and the default signal sent is SIGTERM (terminate).
● Common signals include SIGKILL (kill immediately, cannot be ignored), SIGSTOP
(pause the process), and SIGHUP (reload the process configuration).
Description of package management
● Know the name of the software you want to install.
● Use the appropriate package manager for your Linux distribution (e.g., apt for
Debian/Ubuntu, yum for CentOS/RHEL, dnf for Fedora).
● It’s often a good practice to update the package database before installation,
typically done with commands like sudo apt update or sudo yum check-update.
● Use the installation command specific to the package manager (e.g., sudo apt install
package_name or sudo yum install package_name).
● Check if the software is installed correctly by running it or checking its version.
● Determine the exact name of the software package to be uninstalled.
● Utilize the corresponding uninstallation command for your package manager (e.g.,
sudo apt remove package_name for apt, or sudo yum remove package_name for
yum).
● Some package managers allow the option to remove configuration files as well
(e.g., sudo apt purge package_name).
● Check if the package has been successfully uninstalled by verifying it with the
package manager or checking the software's availability.
● Use commands like dpkg -l package_name for Debian-based systems or rpm -q
package_name for RPM-based systems to check if a specific package is installed.
● Use dpkg -l for Debian-based systems or rpm -qa for RPM-based systems to list all
installed packages.
● Many package managers also have GUI tools (like Synaptic for apt) that allow users
to view installed packages visually.

● Ifconfig is a command-line tool used in Unix-based systems (like Linux) to configure
network interfaces and view network settings such as IP address, subnet mask, and
MAC address.

● Netstat is a command-line tool that displays network connections, routing tables,

● Nslookup is a command-line tool used to query DNS (Domain Name System) to
obtain the domain name or IP address mapping. It helps troubleshoot DNS-related
issues.

● The uname -a command displays comprehensive system information, including the

name, the processor type, and the operating system.
● This information is useful for system administrators to quickly understand the

● It is important for monitoring system memory usage and performance.
● The system_profiler command is specific to macOS and provides detailed
information about the hardware and software of the system.
● It gathers data on hardware specifications (CPU, memory, storage), software
versions (macOS version, installed applications), and setwork configurations.

-- 61 of 132 --

● The sysctl -a command displays all kernel parameters and their current values.

● This command helps system administrators understand and tune system settings

Key readings 2.2.1:Description of Linux files and directories
1. Directory Structure
✓ Root Directory (/): The top-level directory of the Linux file system hierarchy. All
other directories are subdirectories of /.
Example: /home, /etc, /var.
✓ Home Directory (/home): Contains personal directories for each user. For
example, /home/john would be the home directory for user john.
✓ Root User’s Home Directory (/root): The home directory for the root user
(superuser). It is separate from /home for security reasons.
✓ System Directories
/bin: Contains essential user binaries (commands) that are needed for basic
system operation and repair. Examples: ls, cp, mv.
/sbin: Contains system binaries used for system administration. These are
typically used by the root user. Examples: shutdown, ifconfig.
/etc: Contains system-wide configuration files and shell scripts. Examples:
/etc/passwd, /etc/fstab.

/var: Contains variable data like logs, mail spools, and temporary files that
are expected to grow in size. Examples: /var/log, /var/spool.
/tmp: Holds temporary files that are created by various programs. These
files are usually deleted upon reboot or after a certain period.
/dev: Contains device files that represent hardware components and
drivers. These are not regular files but rather interfaces to hardware.
Examples: /dev/sda (a disk), /dev/tty (a terminal).
/proc: A virtual file system that provides information about system
processes and hardware. Examples: /proc/cpuinfo (CPU information),
/proc/meminfo (memory usage).
/sys: A virtual file system that exposes kernel and device information.
o Usage: Provides a way to interact with the kernel and devices, often
used by system tools and utilities.
/usr: Contains user utilities and applications. It is the primary directory for
user software and libraries. Examples: /usr/bin, /usr/lib.
/opt: Used for installing third-party applications and software packages.
/mnt and /media: Used for mounting file systems, such as external drives
or network file systems.
2. File Permissions and Ownership
✓ File Permissions
Read (r): Allows viewing the contents of the file.
Write (w): Allows modifying the file.
Execute (x): Allows executing the file if it is a script or program.
✓ Permission Notation
Symbolic Notation: rwxr-xr,
Explanation: rwx (owner), r-x (group), r-- (others).
Octal Notation: 755
Explanation: 7 (owner: read, write, execute), 5 (group: read, execute), 5
(others: read, execute).
✓ Changing Permissions
chmod Command: Used to change file permissions.
Example: chmod 755 file.txt sets the permissions to rwxr-xr-x.
✓ Changing Ownership
chown Command: Used to change the owner and group of a file.
Example: chown user: group file.txt changes the owner to user and the
group to group.
3. Special Files and Links
✓ Symbolic Links: A symbolic link is a file that points to another file or directory.
Creation: ln -s target linkname

Example: ln -s /etc/hosts myhosts creates a symlink myhosts pointing to
/etc/hosts.
✓ Hard Links: A hard link is another name for an existing file on the file system. It
refers to the same inode.
Creation: ln target linkname
Example: ln file1 file2 creates a hard link file2 to file1.
4. Managing Files and Directories
✓ Creating and Deleting Directories
Create Directory: mkdir directory_name
Remove Directory: rmdir directory_name (empty directory) or rm -r
directory_name (directory with contents)

• Create a directory and its parent directories: If you want to create a directory

1. Creating a New User
The primary command for creating new users in Linux is useradd. You can also use
adduser (which is a more user-friendly frontend to useradd in some distributions).
Basic Syntax:
sudo useradd [options] username
2. Key Attributes to Define for a User
When creating a user, several attributes can be set:
2.1 Username
The username is the identifier for the user in the system.
• Example: Create a new user john.
sudo useradd john
2.2 User ID (UID)
The UID is a unique numerical identifier for the user. By default, the system assigns
the next available UID.
• To assign a specific UID: sudo useradd -u 1050 john
2.3 Primary Group
When a user is created, a primary group is also created by default. You can also
assign the user to an existing group.
• To specify a primary group: sudo useradd -g groupname john
2.4 Secondary Groups
Practical Activity 2.3.2: Creating user attributes

64 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
A user can belong to multiple groups, which help manage access to files and
resources.
• To add the user to secondary groups: sudo useradd -G group1,group2 john
2.5 Home Directory
By default, the user’s home directory is created in /home/username. However,
you can specify a custom directory.
• To specify a home directory: sudo useradd -d /path/to/home/directory john
• To ensure the home directory is created automatically: sudo useradd -m john
2.6 Shell
Each user is assigned a default shell, usually /bin/bash or /bin/sh. You can specify
a different shell for the user.
• To assign a shell: sudo useradd -s /bin/bash john
2.7 Password
After creating a user, you need to set a password for the account. The passwd
command is used for this.
• Set a password for the user: sudo passwd john
2.8 User Expiry Date
You can specify an expiry date for the user account. After the expiry date, the user
will no longer be able to log in.
• To set an expiry date (in YYYY-MM-DD format): sudo useradd -e 2024-12-31 john
2.9 Account Inactivity
The inactivity period is the number of days after a password expires that the
account will be disabled.
• Set inactivity period (in days): sudo useradd -f 30 john
3. Modifying User Attributes
If you need to modify an existing user's attributes, you can use the usermod
command.
Syntax: sudo usermod [options] username
Example Modifications:
• Change the user's home directory: sudo usermod -d /new/home john
• Add the user to a new secondary group: sudo usermod -aG newgroup john
• Change the user's shell: sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh john
4. Deleting a User
To delete a user, the userdel command is used.
• To remove a user without deleting their home directory: sudo userdel john
• To remove the user and their home directory: sudo userdel -r john
5. Viewing User Attributes
• Check User Details: You can view user attributes by inspecting the /etc/passwd
file.
cat /etc/passwd

-- 73 of 132 --

Each user has an entry that includes their username, UID, GID (group ID), home

• Check Group Membership: You can check which groups a user belongs to using
the groups command: groups john
• Check Expiry Date: You can view the account's expiry date using the chage
command: sudo chage -l john
6. User Configuration Files
Some key files that define user attributes and settings include:
• /etc/passwd: Contains user account information like username, UID, GID, home
directory, and shell.
• /etc/shadow: Contains encrypted password information and details about
account expiration.
• /etc/group: Defines the groups and lists the members of each group.
7. Additional Attributes and Settings
You can also configure advanced user attributes related to system resource limits,
such as CPU usage, memory limits, etc., using configuration files like
/etc/security/limits.conf.

Description of user management
● Login Name is unique identifier assigned to each user in the Linux system, often
referred to as the username.
● Identification used for user authentication and to control access to resources.
● Format consists of alphanumeric characters, underscores, and cannot exceed a
certain length (usually 32 characters).
● File Storage for Login names are stored in the /etc/passwd file alongside user
information.
● Encrypted Password are stored in an encrypted format rather than as plain text to
enhance security.
● Uses cryptographic hash functions (e.g., SHA-512) to convert passwords into a
fixed-length string, making it difficult for attackers to retrieve the original
password.
● Encrypted passwords are usually stored in the /etc/shadow file, which is only
accessible by the root user.
● Protects user accounts from unauthorized access, ensuring that even if the
password file is compromised, the actual passwords remain secure.
● UID (User ID) is a unique numerical identifier assigned to each user in the system.
It helps the operating system track user permissions and ownership of files.
● GID (Group ID) is unique numerical identifier assigned to each user group. It
determines the access rights for all users within that group.
● Both UIDs and GIDs are used to enforce file permissions, control access to
resources, and facilitate multi-user environments.
● The root user typically has a UID of 0, while regular users start from UID 1000.
● The command-line interface that is loaded for a user when they log in. Common
shells include /bin/bash, /bin/sh, and /bin/zsh.
Points to Remember

-- 81 of 132 --

73 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
● The default shell determines the command syntax, available features (like scripting
capabilities), and the environment (e.g., prompts, aliases).
● Each shell has associated configuration files (e.g., .bashrc, .bash_profile) that allow
users to customize their environment.
● Users can change their default shell using the chsh command or by modifying the
/etc/passwd file.
While creating a new user account in a Linux server choose a unique user ID and
descriptive username for easy identification.
● Ensure the UID is unique and does not conflict with existing UIDs on the system.
● Set the default shell based on the developer's needs (e.g., /bin/bash, /bin/zsh).
● Specify a dedicated home directory for the user to store their files, if needed.
● Assign a secure password for the new user. Ensure it complies with your
organization's password policies.
● Use passwd to set or change the user's password.
● Assign the user to a primary group, often a group with the same name as the user
or a specific group for development.
● Add the user to additional groups as needed (e.g., developers, admin).
● Ensure the user has the correct permissions for their files and directories.
● Manage group ownership and permissions for shared resources.
● Set the user’s shell to one that is compatible with their development environment.
● Set an account expiration date if the user’s access needs to be limited to a specific
period.
● Check the user account details using commands like id, getent passwd, and groups.
● Verify that the home directory is created and has the correct ownership and
permissions.
● Understand how to lock and unlock user accounts as needed.
● Keep track of user activities and changes to the account for security auditing.
● Document the user’s account details, including username, UID, GID, and groups.
● Inform the developer of their new account details and any relevant instructions for
accessing the server.
Description of group management
● A group name is an identifier for a collection of users.
● It is used to manage permissions and access controls for files and resources.
● Group names can be used in commands to apply the same permissions or settings
to multiple users at once.

-- 82 of 132 --

74 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
● GID (Group ID) is a unique numerical identifier assigned to each group in the
system.
● It is used by the operating system to manage group memberships and permissions.
● Each group has a corresponding GID that differentiates it from other groups.
● Group members are the users who belong to a specific group.
● You can list members of a group by examining the /etc/group file or using
commands like getent group <groupname>.
● Being a member of a group grants users the permissions associated with that group.
● A group password allows users to join a group if they know the password,
enhancing access control.
● This feature is rarely used in modern systems, as managing access through user and
group permissions is typically sufficient.
● Group passwords are set in the /etc/group file but may not be relevant for all
distributions.
● Group ownership refers to the association of a file or directory with a specific
group.
● The group ownership can affect the access permissions of the file for users
belonging to that group.
● You can change the group ownership of a file using the chgrp command.
● Group permissions determine what actions members of the group can perform on
a file or directory (read, write, execute).
● Permissions are set using the chmod command, and the group permissions can be
viewed using ls -l.
● Group permissions can help manage access to shared resources among users.
● A group expiration date can be set to limit the time a group can exist or to restrict
access to the group after a certain date.
● The expiration date can be managed using commands like chage or by editing the
/etc/gshadow file.
● Setting expiration dates is useful for temporary groups or project-based access.
While creating group attributes consider:
• choose a meaningful and descriptive name for the group that reflects its purpose
(e.g., dev_team, admins).
● Ensure that the Group ID is unique and does not conflict with other groups. You can
either assign a specific GID or let the system automatically allocate one. Use the
groupadd -g GID groupname command if you need to specify a GID.
● Each user has one primary group. When a user creates files, the group ownership
defaults to their primary group.

-- 83 of 132 --

75 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
● Users can belong to multiple secondary groups. Add users to the group with the
usermod -aG groupname username command.
● Make sure that adding a user to a group doesn’t remove them from existing groups
by using the -aG option.
● Ensure that directories or files that the group should manage have their group
ownership set correctly.
● Define read, write, and execute permissions for the group. Group permissions
control what actions users in the group can perform on files and directories.
● If a directory is used by multiple users, setting the setgid permission ensures that
new files and subdirectories created within inherit the group ownership.
Description of user and group management
● Managing users and groups is essential for maintaining system security, ensuring
proper access, and organizing users.
● Creates a user with UID 1002, adds them to the developers group, and sets their
default shell to bash.
● Modify existing user attributes, such as adding them to a secondary group.
● Manage file and directory permissions for users and groups.
While managing users and groups:
● Use useradd to create new users and specify important attributes like home
directory (-m), default shell (-s), and user password (passwd).
● Ensure that each user is given the appropriate login environment and permissions.
● Use groupadd to create groups based on departmental or role-based needs.
● Assign users to groups using usermod -aG to manage access controls more
efficiently.
● Ensure that each user is added to the correct group for their department, ensuring
access to shared resources and limiting unauthorized access to sensitive data.
● Use chmod and chown to control access to files and directories.
● Set appropriate permissions based on department requirements with 770 for
directories that need to be private within a department and 777 for directories that
should be accessible to all users (like shared collaboration spaces).
● Create shared directories with open permissions (chmod 777) for collaboration.
● Ensure sensitive files are stored in department-specific directories with restricted
access.
● Regularly update group memberships as users join or leave the organization.
● Change user passwords periodically for enhanced security.
● Use gpasswd -d to remove users from specific groups when needed.

-- 84 of 132 --

76 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
● Test permissions for users to ensure they can only access authorized directories.
● Use commands like cd to verify that users are blocked from unauthorized areas and
have proper access to shared resources.
A team of developers is working on a shared project. All team members should have
read/write access to the project folder, but other users should only have read access.
Your tasks are:
a) Create a new group for the development team.
b) Add the developers to the group.
c) Change the ownership and permissions of the project folder so that the devteam
group can modify files.
d) Ensure other users have only read access

Indicative content 2.4: Application of files and directories permissions
1: Answer the following questions:
i. What does the read permission allow a user to do with a file or directory in a Linux
system?
ii. How does the write permission affect a user's ability to interact with files and
directories in Linux?
iii. What is the significance of the execute permission for files and directories in a
Linux environment?
iv. Explain how symbolic notation is used to represent file permissions in Linux,
including the meaning of r, w, and x.
v. How is octal notation used to represent file permissions in Linux, and what does
the octal number 755 signify for a file or directory?
2: Present the findings to trainer, your colleagues or to the whole class
3: Ask questions where necessary.
4: Read the key readings 2.4.1
Key readings 2.4.1:Description of files and directories permissions
Types of Permissions:
• Read (r): Allows a file to be read or viewed.
• Write (w): Allows a file to be modified.
• Execute (x): Allows a file to be executed (run as a program/script) or a directory
to be accessed (e.g., changing into it with cd).
2. Permission Levels:
• User/Owner (u): The individual who owns the file or directory.
• Group (g): A set of users who share access to the file or directory.
• Others (o): All other users on the system who are not the owner or part of the
group.
3. Viewing Permissions:
Duration: 15 hrs
Theoretical Activity 2.4.1: Description of files and directories permissions
Tasks:

-- 86 of 132 --

78 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
• Use the ls -l command to view the permissions of files and directories. It shows
a string like rwxr-xr-- representing permissions for owner, group, and others
respectively.
4. Changing Permissions (chmod):
• Permissions can be altered using chmod either:
o Symbolically (e.g., chmod u+r to add read permission for the user).
o Numerically (e.g., chmod 755, where each digit represents the
permissions for user, group, and others in the form of a sum: r=4, w=2,
x=1).
5. Changing Ownership (chown):
• Ownership of a file or directory can be changed using the chown command. This
includes:
o Changing the user (e.g., chown user filename).
o Changing the group (e.g., chown user:group filename).
6. Special Permissions:
• Setuid (s): Applied to executables, allows users to execute the file with the
permissions of the file's owner.
• Setgid (s): Applied to files or directories, causes new files to inherit the group of
the directory.
• Sticky Bit (t): Used on directories to ensure only the file owner can delete or
modify files, even if other users have write permissions.
7. Directory Permissions:
• Read (r): Allows users to list the contents of a directory.
• Write (w): Allows users to create, delete, or rename files within the directory.
• Execute (x): Allows users to enter or access the directory, enabling cd to the
directory.
8. Recursive Permission Changes:
• To change permissions for all files and directories within a directory, use the -R
(recursive) option with chmod or chown.
9. Sticky Bit Use Case:
• Commonly applied to shared directories like /tmp. It ensures that users can only
delete or modify their own files within the directory.
10. Default Permissions (umask):
• The umask command sets the default permissions for newly created files and
directories. It subtracts permissions from the maximum possible (usually 666 for
files and 777 for directories).
11. Setting Group Permissions with g+s:
• Applying the setgid (g+s) on a directory ensures all files created in the directory
inherit the group of the directory rather than the user’s primary group.
12. Limiting Access:

-- 87 of 132 --

79 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
• To ensure only specific users or groups can modify files, but everyone else has
only read access:
1: Individual, perform the following activity:
You are the system administrator for a small web development team of five developers
working on a shared project. Your task is to configure permissions for a shared project
directory so that:
a) The developers can collaborate by editing files within the shared directory.
b) Other users on the server should only have read access to the directory.
c) Developers should be able to create and edit files without needing to manually
adjust permissions each time. 2: Read the key reading 2.4.2
3: Configure Permissions on file and directories
4: Present your work to the trainer and your classmate
4: Perform the task provided in application of learning 2.4
Key readings 2.4.2: Applying files and directories permissions
1. Understanding Linux Permissions:
• File Permissions: Each file in Linux has three types of permissions:
o Read (r): Allows viewing the content of the file.
o Write (w): Allows modifying the content of the file.
o Execute (x): Allows running the file as a program (for executable files).
• Directory Permissions: For directories, the permissions have specific meanings:
o Read (r): Allows listing the contents of the directory.
o Write (w): Allows creating, deleting, or renaming files within the
directory.
o Execute (x): Allows accessing the directory (navigating into it).
2. Checking Current Permissions:
• Use the ls -l command to view the permissions of files and directories. The output
will look like this: drwxr-xr-- 2 user group 4096 Sep 29 10:00 mydirectory
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 123 Sep 29 10:00 myfile.txt
• The first character indicates whether it's a directory (d) or a file (-). The next nine
characters are the permissions for user, group, and others.
3. Creating Users and Groups:
• Create Groups: Use the groupadd command to create new groups as needed.
Practical Activity 2.4.2: Applying files and directories permissions
Task:

-- 88 of 132 --

80 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
For example: sudo groupadd devteam
• Add Users to Groups: Use usermod to add users to a group:
sudo usermod -aG devteam username
4. Creating Directories and Files:
• Create directories for projects or shared resources: sudo mkdir
/path/to/project_directory
• Create files within those directories: sudo touch
/path/to/project_directory/file.txt
5. Changing Ownership:
• Change the Owner: Use chown to change the owner of a file or directory: sudo
chown username /path/to/file
• Change Group Ownership: Use chown with the group option: sudo chown
:groupname /path/to/directory
6. Setting Permissions with chmod:
• Symbolic Mode: Use chmod with letters to change permissions: sudo chmod
u+rwx,g+rx,o+r /path/to/directory # User gets read/write/execute, group gets
read/execute, others get read
• Numeric Mode: Use numbers to set permissions (where r=4, w=2, x=1):
sudo chmod 775 /path/to/directory # 7=4+2+1 for user, 7=4+2+1 for group, 5=4+1 for
others
7. Setting Special Permissions:
• Setgid (g+s): Ensures files created in a directory inherit the group of the
directory: sudo chmod g+s /path/to/directory
• Setuid (s): Allows users to execute a file with the permissions of the file’s owner:
sudo chmod u+s /path/to/executable
• Sticky Bit (t): Typically used on directories to allow only the owner to delete or
rename files: sudo chmod +t /path/to/directory
8. Verifying Permissions:
• After applying permissions, verify them using:
ls -ld /path/to/directory
ls -l /path/to/directory
9. Testing Access:
• Log in as different users or switch users using the su command to test whether
permissions are correctly applied: su - username
• Attempt to read, write, or execute files as different users to ensure permissions
are functioning as intended.
10. Monitoring and Auditing:
• Set up logging to monitor file access and changes, which can help in auditing and
security:
sudo apt install auditd

Description of files and directories permission
● The read permission allows a user to view the contents of a file or directory, a user
with read permission can open and read the file's contents, and a user with read
permission on a directory can list the files and subdirectories within it.
● The write permission allows a user to modify a file or directory, a user with write
permission can edit, delete, or create new content in the file, and a user with write
permission can add, remove, or rename files and subdirectories within the
directory.
● The execute permission allows a user to run a file as a program or script, a user
with execute permission can execute the file, provided it is a script or a binary
executable, and a user with execute permission on a directory can access the
directory's contents and perform actions on the files within it (but not necessarily
list them unless they also have read permission).
● Symbolic notation uses letters to represent permissions: r (read), w (write), and x
(execute) and permissions are typically represented in a string of 10 characters,
such as -rwxr-xr--.
● Octal notation is a numerical representation of file permissions, using numbers to
indicate permission levels, and each permission type corresponds to a specific value
Read = 4, Write = 2, and Execute = 1

• Ensure that all developers are members of the devteam group to facilitate
collaboration.
• The shared project directory is set up at the specified path
(/path/to/shared/project). Confirm that all team members are aware of this
location.
• The directory permissions are set to 775, allowing owner and group to read, write,
and execute permissions and others to read-only permissions.
• The setgid bit is applied to the project directory, ensuring that any new files or
directories created within inherit the group ownership of devteam.
• Newly created files in the shared directory will automatically have the group set
to devteam, which means developers won't need to manually adjust permissions
for each new file.
• Other users on the server will only have read access to the shared project
directory and its files, maintaining security and preventing unauthorized
modifications.
• Regularly communicate with the team about the directory usage and any changes
in group membership or permissions.
• Periodically check the permissions and ownership of the project directory to
ensure they remain correctly configured, especially after any system updates or
changes.
• Establish a backup strategy for the project directory to safeguard against data loss.
This may include regular snapshots or backups to a separate storage location.
● Document the changes made, including the creation of the devteam group, the
directory path, and the applied permissions for future reference and onboarding
new team members.

4. To configure common DNS records within the DNS zone files
• Zone file location: Typically located in /var/named/ or /etc/bind/.
• A record: Maps a domain to an IP address.
• MX record: Defines mail server for the domain.
• PTR record: Used for reverse DNS lookup (in reverse zone file).
• SOA record: Defines the Start of Authority, which should be properly
configured for each zone.
5. Testing tools:
• Use dig to query specific DNS records: dig example.com A or dig -x
192.168.1.10 for reverse lookup.
• Use nslookup to test domain resolution: nslookup example.com.
• Check DNS service status: Run systemctl status named (or bind9) to check if
the DNS service is active.
• Log file checks: Look into DNS logs (/var/log/messages or /var/log/syslog) for
any error messages or query logs.
• Syntax checks: Use named-checkconf for configuration file syntax and named-
checkzone to validate zone file correctness.

Key readings 3.2.1.: Description of DHCP services
1. Description of DHCP Handshake Operations
• DHCP Discovery: Client broadcasts a request to find a DHCP server.
• DHCP Offer: DHCP server responds with an IP address offer and network
settings (subnet mask, gateway, DNS, etc.).
• DHCP Request: Client selects an offer and sends a request to the server,
asking to use the provided IP.
• DHCP Acknowledgment: DHCP server confirms the IP assignment and sends
a final acknowledgment, completing the handshake.
2. Install DHCP Server Package
• Linux Systems: Use isc-dhcp-server for Linux-based systems like Ubuntu.
o Install with: sudo apt-get install isc-dhcp-server
• Windows Systems: The DHCP server role is installed via the Server Manager
or PowerShell.
• Ensure the server has a static IP: Dynamic IP on the DHCP server itself may
cause issues during network configuration.
3. DHCP Configuration Files
• Location:
✓ Linux: /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf is the primary configuration file.
✓ Windows: Managed through the DHCP Manager GUI or PowerShell.

• IP Range: Set the range of IP addresses to be assigned to clients.
o Example: range 192.168.1.100 192.168.1.200;
• Lease Time: Define default and maximum lease times to control how long IP

• Network Details: Include the subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server
options.
o Example: option routers 192.168.1.1; option domain-name-servers
192.168.1.20;
• Domain Name: Set the domain name to be assigned to clients.
o Example: option domain-name "mv_tvet.ac.rw";
• Static IP Reservations: Reserve specific IPs for important devices (servers,
printers) by mapping MAC addresses to IP addresses.

Key readings 3.2.2: Configuring DHCP services
1. Description of DHCP Handshake Operations: The DHCP handshake involves a
sequence of messages between a DHCP client and server:
• Discovery: The client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER message to find available
DHCP servers.
• Offer: The server responds with a DHCPOFFER message, offering an IP
address and other network configurations.
• Request: The client responds with a DHCPREQUEST message, requesting the
offered IP address.
• Acknowledgment: The server sends a DHCPACK message, confirming the IP
address allocation and providing the client with network settings.
• Install DHCP Server Package: On a Linux system, you can typically install the
DHCP server package using a package manager.
2. DHCP Configuration Files: The main configuration file for the DHCP server is
usually located at /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf. This file contains settings for network
pools, leases, and options.
3. Set the DHCP Server Parameters: Configure the DHCP server by editing the
configuration file (/etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf). You need to set parameters such as:
• Subnet: Define the subnet and IP address range.
• Range: Specify the range of IP addresses to be assigned to clients.
• Options: Set options like default gateway, DNS servers, and lease time.

# Indicative content 3.3: Configuration of File Server Service

Indicative content 3.3: Configuration of File Server Service
1: Answer the following questions:
i. What is SMB/CIFS, and how is it typically used in network environments?
ii. Explain the role of NFS in file sharing on Unix/Linux networks?
iii. What is FTP, and how does it differ from other file sharing protocols like SMB and
NFS?
2: Present the findings to trainer, your colleagues or to the whole class
3: Address any questions or concerns
4. Read key reading 3.3.1 in their manuals.
Key readings 3.3.1: Description of file Server service
1. Definition of SMB/CIFS
SMB/CIFS is a network file sharing protocol primarily used for sharing files,
printers, and serial ports between systems, especially in Windows
environments.
2. Key Features:
• Cross-Platform Support: Although originally designed for Windows, SMB is
now supported on multiple platforms, including Linux and macOS.
• Authentication: Supports user authentication to control access to shared
resources.
• File and Record Locking: Prevents multiple users from editing the same file
simultaneously, ensuring data integrity.
• Versioning: SMB has several versions, such as SMBv1, SMBv2, and SMBv3,
with newer versions offering better security and performance.
• Encryption: SMBv3 introduces encryption to protect data in transit,
reducing the risk of eavesdropping.
• Windows Integration: Tight integration with Active Directory (AD) for
managing user permissions and access controls.
3. Considerations:
• Ensure that SMBv1 is disabled as it has known security vulnerabilities.
• SMB is chattier (higher network overhead) compared to other protocols.
Duration: 7 hrs

• Firewall settings should be configured to allow SMB ports (445 for direct
SMB and 139 for NetBIOS over TCP).
4. NFS (Network File System): NFS is a file-sharing protocol widely used in
UNIX/Linux environments to share directories and files across a network.
5. Key Features:
• Stateless Protocol: NFS is designed to be stateless, meaning the server
doesn’t maintain session information for clients. This makes it easier to
recover from client or server failures.
• File Locking: NFS provides optional support for file locking, ensuring that
concurrent file access doesn’t lead to data corruption.
• Permissions and Access Control: NFS relies on the Unix permissions system
(UIDs and GIDs) to manage access control.
• Versions: NFS has several versions (NFSv3, NFSv4), with NFSv4 offering
improvements in security (support for Kerberos authentication) and
performance.
• Integration with Linux: It is highly integrated into Linux and UNIX operating
systems and works well in environments where centralized file storage is
needed.
6. Considerations:
• Firewall Configuration: Ensure that the required NFS ports (111, 2049) are
open.
• Security: Use NFSv4 for better security (Kerberos-based authentication)
and encrypted file transfers.
• UID/GID Mapping: Ensure proper user ID mapping between clients and
servers to avoid permission issues.
• NFS might not perform well in environments where there is high network
latency due to its stateless nature.
7. FTP (File Transfer Protocol): FTP is a standard protocol used for transferring files
between a client and server over a TCP-based network, such as the internet.
8. Key Features:
• Basic Authentication: FTP uses simple username and password
authentication, though these credentials are transmitted in plaintext.
• Active vs. Passive Mode: FTP supports two communication modes—active
and passive. In active mode, the client opens a port for data transfer, while
in passive mode, the server opens the port.
• Anonymous FTP: Allows users to download public files from servers
without providing login credentials.
• File Transfer: FTP is ideal for large file transfers and supports both binary
and ASCII modes for file transmission.

-- 112 of 132 --

104 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
• Directory Navigation: FTP allows users to navigate the server’s directory
structure and upload/download files.
9. Considerations:
• Security: FTP is inherently insecure as it transmits data, including
passwords, in plaintext. For secure file transfers, consider using SFTP
(Secure FTP) or FTPS (FTP over SSL).
• Firewall Configuration: Ensure appropriate ports (21 for command, 20
for data) are open, and configure firewalls accordingly for passive/active
modes.
• Encryption: Use FTPS or SFTP to encrypt data in transit for sensitive
information.
10. FTP has high latency sensitivity, meaning network delays can negatively affect
performance, especially in high-latency environments.

Description of file Server service
● SMB (Server Message Block) is a protocol for sharing files, printers, and other
resources, primarily in Windows environments but supported across platforms like
Linux through Samba. CIFS is a dialect of SMB used for file sharing over the internet.
● SMB/CIFS provides features like user authentication, access control, and remote
file access. It operates over TCP/IP (port 445) and supports both TCP and UDP
communication.

● NFS (Network File System) is a distributed file system primarily used in Unix/Linux
environments for file sharing. It is stateless, uses port 2049, and is suitable for data
centers and environments requiring centralized data access.
● FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is focused on file transfers, ideal for
uploading/downloading files between hosts. It operates over port 21 for
commands and uses additional ports for data transfer.
● Differences: SMB/CIFS and NFS focus on file sharing and resource management,
whereas FTP is designed for file transfers. SMB/CIFS is common in Windows, NFS in
Linux/Unix, and FTP is platform-independent but widely used in web hosting.

verifying file access
● Install an FTP server package (e.g., vsftpd or proftpd) using the package manager
(apt install vsftpd or yum install vsftpd).
● Edit the FTP configuration file (e.g., /etc/vsftpd.conf) to set parameters like
anonymous access, local user permissions, and file directories.
● Ensure that the FTP service starts automatically after system boot and is running
properly.
● Open FTP ports (21 for command, 20 for data). Configure firewall rules for active or

Key readings 3.4.1.: Description of web server
1. Definition of a Web Server
A web server is software or hardware that stores, processes, and delivers web pages
to clients (browsers) over the internet using HTTP/HTTPS protocols. It serves static
or dynamic content (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, etc.) requested by users.
2. Types of Web Servers for Linux:
• Apache HTTP Server: The most popular open-source web server known for
its flexibility and wide use. It supports dynamic content via modules.
• Nginx: A lightweight, high-performance web server with a strong focus on
concurrency and low resource usage. It excels at handling large numbers of
simultaneous connections.
• Other Servers: Lighttpd, Caddy, and OpenLiteSpeed also offer web serving
capabilities for specific use cases.
3. Configuration Files: The configuration files for web servers define settings such
as ports, document roots, server names, and security rules.
• Apache: /etc/apache2/apache2.conf or /etc/httpd/httpd.conf
• Nginx: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf or /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

• Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install nginx
• CentOS/RHEL: sudo yum install nginx
• Start and enable it on boot: sudo systemctl start nginx.
6. Firewall Configuration:
• Open ports for HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443) to allow web traffic:
• UFW (Ubuntu): sudo ufw allow 'Apache Full' or sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'
• FirewallD (CentOS): sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent and
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent.

displayed.

• Apache: sudo systemctl status apache2
• Nginx: sudo systemctl status nginx
8. Permissions:
• Ensure proper permissions are set for the web server’s root directory
(/var/www/html) to prevent unauthorized access:
• Ownership: sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html
• Permissions: sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html
• Only allow the web server user (e.g., www-data) write access to sensitive
files.
9. Encryption:
• Protect web server communication by using SSL/TLS encryption to secure
data transferred between the server and clients.
• Use strong ciphers and SSL/TLS protocols to minimize security
vulnerabilities.

Indicative content 3.5: Configuration of Mail Server Service
1: Answer the following questions:
i. What are the key components of an email server, and what roles do they play
in the email delivery process?
ii. What log files are important for monitoring the email server, and what key
metrics should you track for performance and troubleshooting?
iii. What methods can you use to test the functionality of the email server, and
how can you optimize its performance for better efficiency?
iv. What strategies should be employed to ensure regular backups of the email server,
and what steps are necessary to recover from a disaster?
2: Present your findings to the trainer or the whole class
3: Address any questions or concerns.
5: Read the Key readings 3.5.1 in their manuals
Key readings 3.5.1: Description of Mail server services
• SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol): Protocol used for sending emails from
client to server and between servers.
• IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol): Allows users to access and manage
their emails directly on the server, supporting multiple device synchronization.
• POP3 (Post Office Protocol): Downloads emails from the server to the local
client, often removing them from the server.
• Mail Transfer Agent (MTA): Software responsible for routing and delivering
email (e.g., Postfix).
• Mail Delivery Agent (MDA): Delivers email to user mailboxes (e.g., Dovecot).
• Mail User Agent (MUA): Client software used by users to send and receive
emails (e.g., Outlook, Thunderbird).
• Set Up of SMTP Server (Postfix)
✓ Installation: Use package manager commands (apt or yum) to install Postfix.

• Use DNS records (MX records) to route email correctly.
2. Installation and Configuration
• Postfix Setup: Install Postfix for outgoing emails (SMTP) and configure it to
handle email for your domain.
✓ Configure /etc/postfix/main.cf for general settings like domain, hostname,
and networks.
✓ Set up virtual mailboxes if supporting multiple domains.
• Dovecot Setup: Install Dovecot for IMAP/POP3 to allow users to retrieve emails.
✓ Configure /etc/dovecot/dovecot.conf to define mail location and user
settings.
3. DNS Configuration
• Set up MX Records in your DNS to point to the mail server's IP address.
• Configure SPF (Sender Policy Framework), DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail),
and DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting &
Conformance) records to improve email deliverability and security.
✓ SPF defines which mail servers are allowed to send emails for your domain.
✓ DKIM helps ensure that email content hasn’t been tampered with.
✓ DMARC provides a way to tell receiving mail servers how to handle messages
that fail SPF or DKIM checks.
4. Security Considerations
• TLS/SSL Encryption: Ensure all email transmissions are encrypted using TLS
(Transport Layer Security). This can be done by configuring Postfix to use SSL/TLS
for SMTP and Dovecot for IMAP/POP3.
✓ Certificates can be generated using Let's Encrypt or any other CA (Certificate
Authority).
• SASL Authentication: Enable SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) to
require user authentication for sending emails, preventing open relay abuse.
• Firewall Settings: Ensure that ports like 25 (SMTP), 587 (SMTP submission), 993
(IMAP), and 995 (POP3) are open only for relevant services.
5. User and Mailbox Management
• Create mail users and set up mailboxes. Users can be system accounts or virtual
users, depending on your setup.
• For virtual users, configure Postfix to use a virtual mailbox system, often stored
in /var/mail/ or /home/mailboxes/.
6. Spam Filtering and Antivirus
• Set up SpamAssassin or Amavis to filter spam and junk mail.
• Install an antivirus tool like ClamAV to scan emails for malware and other
malicious attachments.
7. Monitoring and Logging
• Regularly monitor mail logs located in /var/log/maillog or /var/log/mail.log for

-- 124 of 132 --

116 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
any issues with email delivery or performance.
• Set up monitoring tools to track email queue length and system performance.
8. Testing the Mail Server
• Use tools like telnet or swaks to test sending and receiving emails from the
server.
• Check that emails are delivered correctly and can be retrieved by users.
• Verify that encryption is correctly applied during email transmission.
9. Backup and Recovery
• Ensure regular backups of the mail server configuration files, user mailboxes, and
important logs.
• Implement a disaster recovery plan that outlines how to restore mail services in
case of failure.
10. User Documentation and Training
• Provide users with the correct settings to configure their email clients (e.g.,
IMAP/POP3 settings, SMTP server, encryption).
• Educate users about strong password usage and how to recognize phishing
emails.
Points to Remember
Description of Mail Server service
● The key components of an email server include SMTP for sending emails,
IMAP/POP3 for receiving, and a mail transfer agent (MTA) like Postfix to manage
the delivery process.
● To install and configure Postfix as an SMTP server on Linux, use package managers
like apt or yum and edit the configuration file (/etc/postfix/main.cf) to set up
domains and relay policies.
● Creating user accounts involves using Linux commands to add users and configuring
their mailboxes in the mail server using tools like Dovecot for IMAP/POP3 access.
● Important log files for monitoring the email server include /var/log/mail.log, where
you track delivery failures, bounce rates, and server load.
● To test email server functionality, you can use commands like telnet or mail clients,
and optimize performance by managing queues and enabling anti-spam measures.
● Regular backups of the email server can be automated using tools like rsync or
backup scripts, and disaster recovery involves restoring configurations, mailboxes,
and ensuring DNS settings are correct.

 Types of Machine Learning
 Supervised Learning
In supervised learning, the model is trained on labeled data, meaning that the input
comes with corresponding correct output labels. The objective is for the model to learn
the mapping between inputs and outputs and predict the output for new, unseen data.
Examples: Classification (e.g., spam detection), Regression (e.g., house price prediction).
Algorithms: Linear Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forests, Support Vector Machines
(SVM), Neural Networks.

 Unsupervised Learning
In unsupervised learning, the model is given data without explicit labels. The goal is to
find patterns, groupings, or structure in the data by analyzing the underlying
relationships.
o Examples: Clustering (e.g., customer segmentation), Dimensionality Reduction (e.g., PCA,
t-SNE).
o Algorithms: K-Means Clustering, Hierarchical Clustering, Principal Component Analysis
(PCA), Autoencoders.
Figure 6: Unsupervised Learning illustration
 Semi-Supervised Learning
o Semi-supervised learning is a hybrid approach where the model is trained on a small
amount of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data. This is useful when labeling
data is expensive or time-consuming.
o Examples: Image classification with few labeled examples.
o Algorithms: Self-training, Co-training, Label Propagation.
Figure 7: Semi-supervised Learning illustration
 Reinforcement Learning
o In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by interacting with an environment. It receives
rewards or penalties based on its actions and learns to maximize cumulative rewards over
time. This approach is used in scenarios where actions influence future states.
o Examples: Game playing (e.g., AlphaGo), Robotics, Autonomous driving.

IoT Sensors: Internet of Things (IoT) sensors are devices that collect and transmit data
about the environment they are monitoring. These sensors can measure various
parameters like temperature, humidity, pressure, motion, light, and more.
Camera: Cameras capture visual data in the form of images and videos. They can be
used in surveillance, monitoring, and recognition systems.
Computer: Computers generate a wide variety of data through different applications,
software, and user interactions. This can include system logs, user activity, application
data, and more.
Smartphone: Smartphones are rich sources of data, generating information from
various sensors (GPS, accelerometer, gyroscope), apps, and user interactions.
Social Data: Social data comes from social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook,
Instagram, LinkedIn, and others. It includes posts, comments, likes, shares, and other
user-generated content.
Transactional Data: Transactional data is generated from business transactions or
operations, typically captured in databases. This data is vital for business operations,
tracking sales, purchases, returns, payments, and more.
 Description of 6 V's of Big Data
The 6 V's of Big Data represent key characteristics that define big data and help in
understanding the complexities involved in managing and analyzing such vast
amounts of information. Here's a description of each:
Volume: Volume refers to the sheer amount of data generated every second
across the globe. It is the most obvious characteristic of big data, as it deals with
vast quantities of data.
Example: Social media platforms generate petabytes of data daily from user
interactions, posts, comments, and likes.
Variety: describes the different types of data that are generated from multiple
sources. Data can be structured, semi-structured, or unstructured.
Example: Data types include text, images, videos, sensor data, log files, emails, social
media posts, and more.
Veracity: refers to the trustworthiness, accuracy, and reliability of the data. This
dimension addresses data quality and the uncertainties present within the data.
Example: Inconsistent data, missing values, and inaccuracies in data sources can lead
to incorrect conclusions if not managed properly.
Value: pertains to the usefulness of the data and the ability to turn big data into
actionable insights that drive business decisions and add value to the organization.

-- 42 of 240 --

Example: Analyzing customer behavior data to improve marketing strategies or using
operational data to optimize supply chain processes.
Variability: refers to the inconsistency of the data flow, which can be affected by
various factors like seasonality, trends, or the context in which the data is
generated.
Example: Retail sales data may vary significantly during holiday seasons compared to
regular days, leading to fluctuating data volumes and types.
Velocity: refers to the speed at which new data is generated, processed, and
analyzed. In the era of real-time data processing, velocity is crucial for timely
decision-making.
Example: Stock market transactions, social media updates, and IoT sensor data are
generated and need to be processed in real-time or near-real-time.
 Description of types of Data
Structured Data: refers to data that is organized in a highly predictable and
predefined manner, typically within a database or spreadsheet. This type of data is
easily searchable and can be stored in tabular forms with rows and columns. Each
field (column) contains a specific type of data (e.g., text, numbers), and each
record (row) is a unique entry.
 Tabular Data: Data organized in rows and columns, like spreadsheets or SQL
databases. Eg.: customer information, financial records, and sensor readings.
 Time-Series Data: Data collected at successive time points, such as stock prices or
weather measurements. Eg.: stock prices, weather data, and website traffic logs.
Examples: Examples: Names, dates, phone numbers, currency or prices, heights or
weights, word count or file size of a document, credit card numbers.
Semi-structured Data is a mix of structured and unstructured data. It does not
reside in a traditional database format (tables and rows), but it does have some
organizational properties, such as tags or markers, that make it easier to process
than unstructured data. Semi-structured data is more flexible than structured data
and can be stored in formats that allow for a variety of data types.
 XML Data: Data marked up with tags, often used in web services.
 JSON Data: Data in JavaScript Object Notation format, commonly used in web
applications.
Examples: Images (both human or and machine-generated), video files, audio files,
social media posts, product reviews, mobile SMS
Unstructured Data refers to data that does not follow a predefined structure or

 Text Data: Data in the form of text, such as articles, emails, or social media posts.
 Image Data: Data consisting of visual information, used in tasks like image

 Audio Data: Data captured in audio formats, like speech & music, used in speech
recognition or audio classification.
 Video Data: Data in the form of video sequences, which is used in video
classification or activity recognition.
Example: Emails, social media posts, multimedia content (images, videos, audio), and

quality, relevance, and size of the dataset significantly influence the performance of
the machine learning model. A well-curated dataset is essential for building accurate
and robust models.
Below are key considerations for gathering datasets:
Define the Objective

clustering, etc.) and the target variable (output).
− Understand Data Needs: Specify what type of data is required (e.g., images, text,
numerical, or a combination).
− Data Quantity: Estimate the amount of data needed to train the model effectively.

Identify Data Sources

Learning Repository, Google Dataset Search, or government databases.
− Sensor Data: Collect data from sensors like temperature, humidity, or
accelerometer readings…
− Web Scraping: Use tools like Beautiful Soup or Scrapy to collect data from
websites.
− APIs: Access data through APIs from services like Twitter API, Google Books API, or
any relevant database.
− Synthetic Data: Generate data using libraries like scikit-learn or faker if real data is
scarce.

Data visualization is the graphical representation of data using charts, graphs,

easily apparent from raw data alone. Visualizations make it easier to
communicate findings, support decision-making, and uncover hidden

animated, and interactive visualizations. It is highly customizable and allows
users to create publication-quality graphs in a variety of formats.

 Applying Data Visualization Best Practices
Creating effective data visualizations requires following certain best practices to ensure
the visuals are clear, engaging, and easy to interpret. Here’s how to apply these best
practices:
 Know Your Audience
Tailor the visualization style to the knowledge level and interests of the audience. For
example, technical audiences may prefer detailed graphs, while non-technical audiences
need simple, easy-to-read visuals.
 Simplify Visuals
Avoid overloading your visualization with excessive details. Simplicity ensures that the
audience can quickly grasp the key message without distractions.

 Choose the Right Chart Type
Selecting the appropriate chart type is crucial for conveying information effectively. For
example, bar charts are better for comparisons, while line charts are suitable for trends
over time.
 Use Appropriate Scales
Ensure axes, labels, and legends are scaled appropriately so that the data is not
misleading.
 Label Clearly
All elements of the visualization, including axes, legends, and titles, should be clearly
labeled for ease of understanding.
 Choose Colors Wisely
Colors are powerful for highlighting important data points, but they can also distract or
mislead if used improperly.
 Avoid Misleading Visualizations
Misleading visuals can distort the message and lead to incorrect conclusions.
 Interpreting Visualization Results
Once visualizations are created, interpreting them correctly is essential to derive
actionable insights. Interpretation involves recognizing patterns, identifying trends, and
understanding relationships in the data.
 Patterns and Trends
Identifying recurring patterns and trends in data visualizations helps make predictions
and understand the data over time or across categories.
Example: A line plot showing the trend of rising sales over months can indicate
growing market demand.
Interpretation:
o Upward Trend: Growth in the variable (e.g., increasing sales or population).
o Downward Trend: Decline in the variable (e.g., decreasing website traffic).
o Seasonal Pattern: Regular fluctuations based on specific times or conditions (e.g.,
retail sales peaking during holidays).

 Correlations and Relationships
Visualizations such as scatter plots and heat maps can reveal correlations between
variables. Correlations help in understanding how one variable might affect or be
associated with another.
Example: A scatter plot showing the relationship between temperature and ice
cream sales can reveal a positive correlation, where higher temperatures lead to
increased sales.
Interpretation:
o Positive Correlation: As one variable increases, the other increases (e.g., higher study
hours leading to higher exam scores).
o Negative Correlation: As one variable increases, the other decreases (e.g., more
rainfall leading to lower water consumption).
o No Correlation: No clear relationship between variables (e.g., shoe size and
intelligence).
o Causation vs. Correlation: Be careful to distinguish between correlation (variables
move together) and causation (one variable causes changes in another).

1.5.2. Characteristics of quality Data in machine learning
High-quality data is critical for accurate analysis and decision-making. Several
characteristics define data quality:
Accuracy:
Accuracy ensures that data values are correct and reflect real-world observations.
Errors in accuracy can lead to incorrect conclusions.
Example: If a dataset contains a column for "age," an entry showing "178"
would be inaccurate, as it’s impossible for a human to live that long.
Completeness:
Data is considered complete if there are minimal or no missing or incomplete entries
that could hinder analysis. Each feature should have sufficient data points to ensure
robust analysis

-- 68 of 240 --

Example: A sales dataset missing the “date of purchase” for several records
would be incomplete and potentially unreliable.
Consistency:
Consistent data means that there are no conflicting values in the dataset, such as
different formats or contradicting entries.
Example: - A dataset with dates in both MM/DD/YYYY and DD/MM/YYYY
formats can lead to confusion and misinterpretation.
- If some entries for "country" are listed as "USA" and others as "United
States," it creates inconsistency. A consistent dataset has similar entries.
Relevance:
Relevance ensures that the data is pertinent and useful for the task or analysis at
hand. Irrelevant data adds noise and may decrease model performance.
Example: Collecting historical weather data when analyzing customer
purchasing behavior might not be relevant.
- If you’re predicting house prices, features like "square footage" and "number
of bedrooms" are relevant, while "favorite color" is not.
Timeliness
Data should be up-to-date and reflect the current state of the environment or
phenomenon it represents, especially in dynamic fields.
Example: A dataset predicting stock prices should use the most recent trading
data. Using old data can lead to inaccurate predictions.
Uniformity
Data should follow a standard format (e.g., date formats, numerical precision). This
includes consistent units of measurement.
Example: If dates are recorded in different formats (e.g., MM/DD/YYYY and
DD/MM/YYYY), it can lead to confusion. A uniform dataset would use one
consistent date format.
Granularity
The data should have an appropriate level of detail. Too much granularity can lead to
noise, while too little can obscure important patterns.
Example: For analyzing customer behavior, data collected daily (daily sales)
might be too granular. Weekly or monthly summaries might provide a clearer
overview without overwhelming detail.

-- 69 of 240 --

Diversity
A diverse dataset captures a wide range of scenarios and variations, which helps the
model generalize better to new, unseen data.
Example: If a model predicting loan approvals is trained on data from only
one demographic group, it may not perform well for others. A diverse dataset
would include various age groups, income levels, and backgrounds.
Non-redundancy
High-quality data should avoid redundancy. Duplicate records can skew results and
lead to overfitting.
Example: If a customer's record appears multiple times in a dataset, it can
skew results. A non-redundant dataset would have each customer listed
once.
Scalability
The dataset should be manageable in size, allowing for efficient processing and
analysis without compromising performance.
Example: A dataset with millions of records may slow down machine learning
algorithms. A scalable dataset is one that can be efficiently processed,
possibly by sampling or aggregating.
Structured
Data should be organized in a clear and logical manner. Structured data (like tables) is
easier to analyze compared to unstructured data (like text).
Example: A structured dataset might be formatted as a table with rows and
columns, such as a CSV file with clear headers like "Name," "Age," and
"Occupation."
Validity:
Data validity ensures that collected data conforms to the defined rules or constraints,
such as data type, range, or specific formats. This means that the data should not
only be accurate and consistent but also relevant to the specific needs of the analysis.
Example: A dataset with an age field containing negative values or characters
(e.g., “-5” or “abc”) would be invalid.

1.5.4. Description of data normalization
1. Definition
Data Normalization is the process of adjusting the values of numeric data to a common
scale, without distorting differences in the ranges of values. The main goal of normalization
is to ensure that each feature contributes equally to the distance calculations in machine
learning algorithms, particularly those sensitive to the scale of data, such as k-nearest
neighbors (KNN) and gradient descent-based algorithms.
2. Importance of Data Normalization
Improves Model Performance: Many machine learning algorithms, especially those
based on distance metrics (like KNN and SVM), perform better when the data is on
a similar scale. Normalization helps in achieving this uniformity.
Accelerates Convergence: In algorithms that use gradient descent for optimization,
such as linear regression and neural networks, normalization can speed up
convergence. It helps the algorithm to reach the optimal solution faster.
Reduces Sensitivity to Input Scale: Normalized data helps in reducing the sensitivity
of models to the scale of input features, making models more robust.
Enhances Interpretability: Normalized data can make it easier to interpret the
results of the model, as the features are on a common scale.
Facilitates Feature Comparisons: When features are normalized, it becomes easier
to compare their effects on the output, aiding in feature selection and engineering.
3. Data Normalization Techniques
Several methods are used for normalizing data, depending on the type of model and the
specific characteristics of the dataset.

-- 73 of 240 --

1. Min-Max Normalization (Rescaling):
This technique scales the data to a fixed range, typically between 0 and 1.
Use Case: Ideal for datasets where the values need to be bounded, and the feature
distribution is not Gaussian (normal distribution).
Example:
 Original data: [5, 10, 15, 20]
 Normalized (0-1): [0, 0.33, 0.67, 1]
2. Z-Score Normalization (Standardization):
This method centers the data around the mean with a standard deviation of 1, making it
suitable for features with a Gaussian distribution.
Use Case: Useful for data with varying scales but a Gaussian distribution. It’s often
used in algorithms like logistic regression and support vector machines (SVM).
Example:
 Original data: [10, 20, 30, 40]
 Mean: 25, Standard deviation: 11.18
 Standardized: [-1.34, -0.45, 0.45, 1.34]
3. Decimal Scaling:
This technique involves moving the decimal point of the values to normalize them. The
scaling factor is determined by the maximum absolute value in the data.
Use Case: Used when the values vary by orders of magnitude, and you want to scale
the data down uniformly.
4. MaxAbs Scaling:
Similar to Min-Max normalization, but here the data is scaled by dividing by the maximum

-- 74 of 240 --

absolute value of each feature. It maintains the sign of the original data.
Use Case: Useful when dealing with sparse data (e.g., in text processing or image
classification), and you want to maintain the distribution's original sign while
scaling.
5. Logarithmic Scaling:
This technique takes the logarithm of the values to reduce the impact of large outliers and
bring skewed distributions closer to normality.
Use Case: Often applied in scenarios where data has exponential growth patterns
(e.g., population growth, economic data).
6. Robust Scaler (Median and IQR Normalization):
This method normalizes data by removing the median and scaling the data according to the
interquartile range (IQR). It’s robust to outliers since it relies on percentiles rather than
mean and variance.
Use Case: Best suited for datasets with many outliers where the standard scaling
techniques would be affected by extreme values.

def extract_rpm(value):
if isinstance(value, str): # Ensure value is a string before processing
# Extract the RPM part from the string
rpm_match = re.search(r'(\d+[-\d]*)(rpm)', value)
if rpm_match:
rpm_str = rpm_match.group(1)
if '-' in rpm_str:
# If there is a range like 1500-2500, take the average
rpm_range = rpm_str.split('-')
rpm_value = (int(rpm_range[0]) + int(rpm_range[1])) / 2
else:
rpm_value = int(rpm_str.replace(",", ""))
return rpm_value
return None # Return None for non-string values

Key readings 2.1.2. Description of Unsupervised Machine Learning algorithm
 Unsupervised Learning Algorithms
Unsupervised Machine learning models implement the learning process opposite to
supervised learning, which means it enables the model to learn from the unlabeled
data.
Figure 50 Unsupervised Algorithms
Unsupervised learning aims to discover the dataset’s underlying pattern, assemble
that data according to similarities, and express that dataset in a precise format.
Let us discuss different unsupervised machine learning algorithms.
 K-Means Clustering
K-Means Clustering is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm used for
partitioning a dataset into distinct groups (clusters) based on similarity.
The objects with the most similarities remain in the same group, and they have no
or very few similarities from other groups.

-- 143 of 240 --

Clustering algorithms can be widely used in different tasks such as Image
segmentation, Statistical data analysis, Market segmentation, etc.
Some commonly used Clustering algorithms are K-means Clustering, hierarchal
Clustering, DBSCAN, etc.
Figure 51 Clustering in K-Means Clustering
 Imagine you're a party planner. You have a list of guests with their addresses,
and you want to divide them into groups so you can send out invitations more
efficiently.
Here's how K-Means Clustering works:
1. Choose the number of groups (clusters): Let's say you want to divide guests
into 3 groups based on their location.
2. Randomly place 3 "party centers" on the map: These are your initial cluster
centers.
3. Assign each guest to the nearest party center: This creates your initial groups.
4. Move each party center to the average location of the guests assigned to it:
This improves the center's position to better represent the group.
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4: Guests are reassigned, and centers are moved again. This
process continues until the centers stabilize, meaning they no longer move
significantly.
The result: You have 3 distinct groups of guests, each centered around a party
location. This allows you to easily send out invitations and plan logistics for each
group.
In essence, K-Means Clustering groups similar data points together by iteratively
finding the centers of those groups.
 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised machine learning technique
primarily used for dimensionality reduction. It transforms a high-dimensional
dataset into a lower-dimensional form while preserving as much variability as

-- 144 of 240 --

possible. PCA is widely used for feature extraction, noise reduction, and data
visualization.
 Let's say you're building a face recognition system. Each face image has
thousands of pixels, making it difficult for a computer to process efficiently.
PCA can help by:
1. Finding the most important facial features: PCA identifies the key features that
distinguish one face from another, such as eye shape, nose size, and jawline.
2. Reducing the number of pixels: PCA can represent each face image with a
smaller set of numbers, capturing the essence of the face while reducing the
amount of data.
This makes face recognition faster and more accurate, as the computer can focus on
the most important information.
 Hierarchical Clustering
In machine learning, clustering is the unsupervised learning technique that groups
the data based on similarity between the set of data.
A dendrogram, a tree-like figure produced by hierarchical clustering, depicts the
hierarchical relationships between groups. Individual data points are located at
the bottom of the dendrogram, while the largest clusters, which include all the
data points, are located at the top. In order to generate different numbers of
clusters, the dendrogram can be sliced at various heights.
The dendrogram is created by iteratively merging or splitting clusters based on a
measure of similarity or distance between data points. Clusters are divided or
merged repeatedly until all data points are contained within a single cluster, or
until the predetermined number of clusters is attained.
We can look at the dendrogram and measure the height at which the branches of
the dendrogram form distinct clusters to calculate the ideal number of clusters.
The dendrogram can be sliced at this height to determine the number of clusters.
Types of Hierarchical Clustering
Basically, there are two types of hierarchical Clustering:
1. Agglomerative Clustering
2. Divisive clustering
I. Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering
It is also known as the bottom-up approach or hierarchical agglomerative clustering
(HAC). A structure that is more informative than the unstructured set of clusters
returned by flat clustering. This clustering algorithm does not require us to
prespecify the number of clusters. Bottom-up algorithms treat each data as a
singleton cluster at the outset and then successively agglomerate pairs of

-- 145 of 240 --

clusters until all clusters have been merged into a single cluster that contains all
data.
Figure 52Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering
Steps:
 Consider each alphabet as a single cluster and calculate the distance of one
cluster from all the other clusters.
 In the second step, comparable clusters are merged together to form a single
cluster. Let’s say cluster (B) and cluster (C) are very similar to each other
therefore we merge them in the second step similarly to cluster (D) and (E) and
at last, we get the clusters [(A), (BC), (DE), (F)]
 We recalculate the proximity according to the algorithm and merge the two
nearest clusters([(DE), (F)]) together to form new clusters as [(A), (BC), (DEF)]
 Repeating the same process; The clusters DEF and BC are comparable and
merged together to form a new cluster. We’re now left with clusters [(A),
(BCDEF)].
 At last, the two remaining clusters are merged together to form a single cluster
[(ABCDEF)].
II. Hierarchical Divisive clustering
It is also known as a top-down approach. This algorithm also does not require
to prespecify the number of clusters. Top-down clustering requires a method
for splitting a cluster that contains the whole data and proceeds by splitting
clusters recursively until individual data have been split into singleton clusters.

predicting house prices based on features like size and location.

spam or not spam.
Clustering: When the goal is to group similar data points together without predefined
labels. For example, customer segmentation based on purchasing behaviour.
